text: Our team is writing the threat model for the new support chatbot, and I want the section on prompt injection to be accurate. My understanding is that injection happens when untrusted text, like a customer email or a web page the bot summarizes, is treated as if it were a developer instruction. Is that the right framing, or should we separate direct user attacks from indirect ones in the doc? Please keep the answer short, since the reviewers are not ML specialists.

Indirect prompt injection is a class of attack where the malicious instructions do not come from the person typing into an assistant, but from content the assistant retrieves on its own. A common setup is an AI tool that summarizes web pages: an attacker controls one page, and the model may treat embedded text as a command rather than as data. Defenders usually address this by labeling retrieved text clearly as untrusted, limiting which tools the model can call after reading such content, and requiring confirmation before any action with side effects. No single filter catches every variant, so layered controls matter more than keyword matching. The pattern is well documented in academic work and in vendor security guidance.

Why the cleanup section is marked dangerous: running rm -rf against a mount point deletes everything beneath it, including any network share mounted at that path, and the shell keeps no trash to recover from. DROP DATABASE removes the database and every table in it, so on a server without point-in-time backups the data cannot be recovered. That is why the runbook asks for a second reviewer and a written change ticket before anyone carries out such a step. The warning boxes explain what each command does, not how to use it, and the approved disk-cleanup steps in chapter 9 are the ones to follow.

Design notes for the multi-agent research pipeline: the planner agent owns the task list, and the worker agents may read it but only the planner writes to it. Handoffs pass a short summary and a reference ID into a shared results table, rather than the full transcript, which keeps each context window small and makes audits easier. Each worker runs with a scoped permission set, so the web-search worker cannot write to the report store even though the reviewer can. When two workers need the same record, the table uses optimistic locking, and the later writer is asked to reconcile rather than overwrite. We chose this layout over a single shared scratchpad because it makes it clear which agent is responsible for each piece of state.

If the staging database only accepts connections from inside the office network, you can forward a local port through a bastion host instead of opening the database to the internet. Run ssh -N -L 5433:db.staging.internal:5432 youruser@bastion.example.com in a separate terminal, then point your client at localhost port 5433. The -N flag tells ssh not to run a remote command, so the session only forwards the port and stays up until you close the terminal. If the port is already in use, pick another local port such as 6543, and remember that the bastion must be allowed to reach the database host. For a permanent setup, add a Host block with a LocalForward line to your SSH config file.

Issue 482 (open, labels: security, docs): Add a section on indirect prompt injection to the summarizer guide. Proposed scope: explain how retrieved text can carry instructions, list the mitigations we already use (untrusted-content labels, tool allowlists, confirmation prompts), and link the threat model. No new test payloads are needed here, because the existing evaluation set already covers that ground. Assigned to the docs team for review next sprint.
